Introduction

Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Device Manufacturer (ODM).

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices.

We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations.

While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure.

Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet:

  • Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules

  • Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor

  • Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors

  • Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices

Overview

The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase.

Figure 1: XCPE malware overview

Malware

Since at least late 2024, Videostrong has evolved its pre-installed malware from simple single-stage droppers into a modular, three-stage architecture designed for resilience and multi-tenant monetization:

  • Primary Backdoor: Operating at the 

    android.uid.system
    privilege level, 
    x.cpe
    (running as 
    com.oemservice
    in some builds) is preloaded in the firmware partition. If uninstalled by a user, it automatically reinstalls from the 
    /oem/
    partition upon reboot, maintaining persistent system-level access. Its main function is to establish and facilitate communications between the C2 server and the loader and execution engine. 

  • Loader and Execution Engine: To evade security scans, 

    x.cpe
    acts primarily as the C2 communicator and offloads module execution to an external loader, 
    com.abc.nexus
    . This file employs native anti-analysis utilities to thwart sandbox detection, and configures and initializes the monetization modules. Most recently, 
    com.abc.nexus
    has itself been phased out in favor of using more tailored dropper malware that loads and executes single modules.

  • Monetization Modules: Videostrong monetizes its backdoored devices by loading monetization modules which are developed by entities other than Videostrong that act as affiliates. These modules are deployed as native ELF daemons, embedded SDKs compiled directly into the 

    com.abc.nexus
    DEX bytecode, or are fetched as secondary APKs from the malware staging infrastructure.  The loaded modules transform infected devices into residential proxy exit nodes (e.g., Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut), ad-fraud engines (e.g., CBOXTV, HiddenView), or execute additional backdoors that load even more monetization modules (e.g. Moyu, Spirit).

Infrastructure

  • Command and Control: The botnet uses a two-stage C2 process. It first initiates HTTP POST requests to fetch dynamic configuration settings, geolocation data, and STUN server parameters. It then establishes a persistent, real-time Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) connection to receive instructions for silent app installations, arbitrary shell commands, screen captures, and network reconnaissance. MQTT is a lightweight, publish-and-subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable remote networks.

Malware staging infrastructure: Additional monetization modules as well as various shell scripts and legitimate applications are hosted remotely and downloaded by infected devices upon command from the operator via the MQTT broker. A significant majority of these files are hosted as Github releases on operator-owned Github pages. Other files are hosted on operator-controlled servers and file hosting sites.

Malware Deep Dive

Backdoor Initialization

The infection chain begins with a stub package (called 

x.cpe
in some builds and 
com.oemservice
in others) preloaded in the system partition of the firmware and running at the 
android.uid.system
privilege level. This stub has limited functionality. Upon boot, it checks the device's 
oem/
directory for the corresponding 
x.cpe
package and initiates installation into the 
/data/app/
directory as outlined below. 

To maintain inter-process state across the firmware ecosystem, 

x.cpe
exports two ContentProviders, which expose structured configuration tables storing runtime parameters, device identifiers, proxy configuration blobs, and execution flags accessible by co-installed system applications. This enables other apps in Videostrong’s ecosystem, such as their YokaTV Player streaming software, to fetch configuration parameters provided by the C2 server mentioned below. 

C2 Configuration

The malware utilizes a two-stage communications protocol. It first fetches initial bootstrap configurations via an HTTP request, followed by a persistent MQTT subscription to receive commands and module download instructions.

To dynamically derive the HTTP C2 bootstrap server, it follows the following routine:

  • Queries 

    content://com.release.debug.provider/configs
    for 
    private_url
    via 
    x.cpe.util.ExtraReadUtils
    . 

  • Queries the Android system property to determine if 

    ro.mecool.device
    is true.

  • If true, it defaults to 

    http://mcstb.anyevonline.com:8000
     

  • If false, it dynamically generates the following: 

    http://stb[AndroidVersion][Type].anyevonline.com:8000
    .

Using the selected hostname, the client makes an HTTP POST request with an AES-encrypted JSON object containing hardware telemetry (SN, MAC, model, firmware version) to the following endpoints:

  • /router/config/mqtt: This endpoint provides MQTT broker details (including Broker Hostname, TCP Port, Authentication Tokens/Passwords, and the specific Topic structure: 

    /device/{model}/{chipId}/{action}
    . After receiving this data, the device initiates a persistent, real-time socket connection to the MQTT broker.

  • /router/config/acs: This endpoint response returns URLs for 

    ip-api[.]com
      and a Google STUN server to enable the malware to identify geolocation and public IP and port mapping to traverse network address translation (NAT) boundaries. It also returns a URL (
    http://ott.szbboys[.]com:8000/cpe/file/upload
    for uploading files, logs, or diagnostic dumps from the device, and returns flags to configure ad modules (
    adBwmActive
    , 
    adDevourUse
    , 
    adDevourCode
    ), and to enable or disable core malware modules.

/router/config/app: This endpoint provides module-level configs, including server mappings and parameters, which 

x.cpe
decrypts and passes to a SQLite 
ContentProvider
named 
ShareProvider
(
com.oem.share.provider
). By exposing this inter-process data interface, 
x.cpe
enables modules to retrieve up-to-date upstream infrastructure parameters (such as URLs for additional configs, user manuals, etc).

MQTT Capabilities

Following initial configuration, persistent real-time C2 communication is managed by the MQTT library (

x.cpe.mqtt.MqttUtils
). All identified samples analyzed to date utilize a single broker hostname, 
mqtt.szbboys[.]com
. 

Specific MQTT topics are mapped to specific actions, including:

  • Silent Application Installation: Fetches remote APKs to a temporary directory.

  • Disable Google Play Protect: To bypass security, 

    AppUtils.disablePackageVerify()
    targets the global setting "
    package_verifier_user_consent
    " via 
    Settings.Global.putInt
    and sets it to 
    -1
    , disabling Google Play Protect app verification.

  • Arbitrary Shell Execution: Executes remote commands via 

    sh
    under system UID privilege level. Results are published to the MQTT broker.

  • Shell Script Execution: Downloads and executes shell scripts via 

    x.cpe.util.RunCmds
    .

  • Remote Desktop Monitor & Screen Capture: Utilizes 

    android.app.Instrumentation.sendKeyDownUpSync()
    to inject keycodes and Java reflection on hidden APIs (
    android.view.SurfaceControl.screenshot
    / 
    SurfaceControl$ScreenshotHardwareBuffer
    ) to continuously capture the screen, compress to JPEG, and publish over MQTT.

  • Network Reconnaissance: Invokes embedded binaries (

    libtraceroute.so
    ) to fingerprint the victim network, and perform standard ping tests. The binaries also perform robust AS-lookup WHOIS routing queries.

Our analysis of the C2 data indicates the preponderance of interactions with victim devices were related to module install, uninstall, and configuration actions. We also observed Videostrong operators executing sensitive actions on the device, including capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive data including account information, device information, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including to establish reverse shells on devices.

Loader and Execution Engine Details

Earlier versions of 

x.cpe
directly embedded malicious monetization modules. In late 2024 – possibly as a response to earlier Google enforcement related to BadBox – Videostrong removed malicious modules from 
x.cpe
and introduced a separate malicious package they developed, 
com.abc.nexus
, which 
x.cpe
routes instructions and data to via Inter-Process Communication (IPC). Modern variants of 
x.cpe
facilitate C2 communications but pass configuration parameters, module updates, and other payloads to 
com.abc.nexus
as the execution engine. We believe the actor may have evolved the malware in this way in an attempt to ensure 
x.cpe
could remain undetected.

Upon boot, 

com.abc.nexus.broadcast.BootReceiver
broadcasts the 
com.abc.nexus.data
intent, bootstrapping 
com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService
. Within 
CoreService.onCreate
, the application performs maintenance and persistence tasks. The main logic sets up a listener through 
RemoteMessageHandler
for IPC communications from 
x.cpe,
and parses JSON payloads received from it.  

After these steps, 

CoreService
initializes the monetization modules. 
com.abc.nexus
services extract and orchestrate a series of nested native libraries and dynamically downloaded secondary payloads which vary significantly based on sample. Many versions of 
com.abc.nexus
come preloaded with four or more embedded modules, while other versions contain as few as one. The most common malware modules include 
TitanService
, 
BwmService
, 
AdtimeService
, 
lb102Service
, and 
LinkfogService
(sometimes called 
AgentService)
. Discussion of these and other modules can be found in the monetization modules section. 

Persistence and Evasion

The malware operators implement a number of mechanisms to establish persistence and thwart detection and analysis.

As a system preload, 

x.cpe
cannot be removed by the user. If 
x.cpe
is uninstalled from 
/data/app/
, upon reboot the 
x.cpe
service 
BootReceiver
follows the same routine outlined above and reinstalls the package. 

The backdoor is able to silently download additional files to the device and execute them without user consent because it first wipes user consent configuration on the device and then disables Google Play Protect:

public static void disablePackageVerify() {
    PreferenceUtils.setPackageVerifyFromUser(CPEApp.instance, true);
    AppUtils.setPackageVerify(-1); // Actioning a bypass against GPP evaluation
}

Figure 2: Disabling Google Play Protect

In many variants of 

com.abc.nexus,
we observed the extraction of a sophisticated anti-analysis and process hardening utility 
libseccomp_guard.so
, which runs prior to the initialization of malware modules, to ensure they remain protected from automated sandboxes and security instrumentation. It filters system calls to prevent the pausing or termination of individual threads, denies cross-process interference to ensure isolation, and prevents the spawning of child processes. 

Evolution

Since August 2026, new dropper packages have been installed via the MQTT channel, which appear to be synchronized with the mass-uninstallation of 

com.abc.nexus
across the botnet. We assess this may represent a new evolution of the malware to further evade detection. These new packages are disguised as Android system applications, with names such as 
com.android.system.ntp
and
 com.android.sso.auth.handler
. Where 
com.abc.nexus
could act as a general purpose loader and execution engine (executing instructions passed to it from 
x.cpe
), these packages instead install single monetization modules (such as AppSalt).  Multiple variants of these packages extract a native ELF file, 
libexploit.so
, which in turn executes functions 
nativeAdbRoot()
and 
nativeAdbShell()
. These functions restart the local 
adbd
service as root, and initiate an ADB shell connection. Following this, the app uses the connection to install itself in the 
system
partition.  The 
system
partition is remounted as read-write and the payload replicates itself to a newly minted directory in 
/system/priv-app/
and creates an XML file at 
/system/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions-.xml
. This file grants the malware 
android.permission.INSTALL_PACKAGES
and 
android.permission.REBOOT
. 

The app configures the malware modules through hardcoded configuration parameters, and does not listen for 

x.cpe
IPC messages. The app itself is controlled by the operators via shell scripts pushed via the broker and executed by 
x.cpe
. These include setting the property 
persist.networkstack.uninstall
(which, when read by the app, triggers uninstallation and cleanup), 
persist.networkstack.skip_system_install
(which skips system installation, forcing it to remain running in 
/data/app/
), and 
persist.networkstack.install_time
(which implements timestomping, overriding the default timestamp of the app to align with the other packages installed in the 
system
directory).  

Botnet composition

The botnet is globally dispersed, with certain concentrations possibly implying market penetration for the brand distributor.

Figure 3: Global distribution of x.cpe

While the overwhelming majority of the infected devices in the XCPE botnet are Android TV set-top boxes, we observed a number of other infected Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

Monetization

x.cpe
loads a variety of malicious modules for monetization. Most often the modules are associated with residential proxy services and bandwidth sharing, but we've also observed ad fraud modules. Given that a single device may be running multiple modules providing the same or similar functionality (e.g., as many as three residential proxy SDKs installed on a single device) it is clear that Videostrong seeks to monetize every infected device to the greatest extent possible. 

Services are loaded by 

com.abc.nexus
via three methods:

  • Native Daemons: Native ELF binaries prepackaged with 

    com.abc.nexus
    , which are unpacked to data directories and spawned as background processes with system/root privileges.

  • Embedded SDKs / Services: Java/Kotlin SDKs compiled directly into Nexus and invoked via Android Service lifecycles or IPC broadcast triggers.

  • Dynamic Droppers & Secondary APK Installers: Downloader function that pulls remote native ELFs or secondary standalone APKs and invokes system package managers. Nexus receives messages from 

    x.cpe
    directing it to download specific modules.

Malware modules loaded via the backdoor include the following:

Residential Proxy / Bandwidth Sharing Modules

LINKFOG

Com.abc.nexus
’s 
LinkfogService
unpacks a Go binary named 
lw_android_agent
  from 
assets/
to local app storage and supplies it with vendor parameters. This service silently turns infected devices into residential edge computing and PCDN proxy exit nodes. It connects to FRP reverse tunnels, and uploads bandwidth accounting metrics to Linkfog API backends. Linkfog (operated by Beijing Linkfog Technology via 点心云 / Dianxinyun) brands itself as a “Peer-to-Peer Content Delivery Network”.

Jaguar

The

 com.abc.nexus
AdtimeService
extracts 
libjaguar.so
from 
assets/
. The file is an unobfuscated 32-bit ELF binary written in C, compiled as a native Android binary. It utilizes JNI (Java Native Interface) to initialize its core routines, dynamically derives a ChaCha20 decryption key via ARM NEON SIMD instructions to decode heavily obfuscated configurations , and establishes an encrypted C2 channel. Upon successful registration, the C2 responds with JSON configuration specifying proxy endpoints. The proxy command loop 
x_ctrl_do_ctrl_msg
delegates proxy operations based on incoming JSON variable commands, and is capable of both TCP and UDP relay.

AppSalt / Honeygain

AppSalt SDK is the residential proxy SDK owned by Honeygain, which is in turn owned by Oxylabs. 

com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService
initializes Appsalt SDK. First, the application obtains an Appsalt SDK API key from a native library 
libnative_keys.so
by calling its 
getAppsaltKey()
function. Appsalt SDK is initialized without displaying a consent screen - instead it explicitly calls the 
optIn()
method which sets a consent flag without displaying any user interface. During Appsalt SDK startup it checks the application's installation source and stops execution if the application was installed from the official Google Play Store. 

Once Appsalt is successfully initialized it establishes a WebSocket connection with the primary command and control domain. Appsalt uses JSON-formatted messages for initial check-in (registration) and heartbeat requests. Appsalt command and control servers use MessagePack formatted messages to issue commands pertaining to proxy operations. Appsalt SDK is configured with an initial set of domains that act as proxy gateways. The list of proxy gateways can be updated by the command and control server. The device establishes UDP / QUIC connections with these gateways.

BWM / IPWeb

This residential proxy and bandwidth-sharing node is implemented through the 

com.abc.nexus.service.BwmService
component (sometimes named 
com.abc.nexus.service.SN4Service)
and its associated SDK. Upon initialization, it secures itself within an isolated sandbox environment, captures device telemetry, and registers with a remote server over UDP. From this C2, it receives instructions to initiate a Java NIO TCP multiplexed proxy tunnel. The service functions to route arbitrary traffic through the infected device on behalf of a remote threat actor.

GaGaNode

GaGaNode is the first-party SDK owned by residential proxy operator IPCola. It connects over TCP to a primary C2 server and sends heartbeat beacon data over HTTP POST to a separate server. The SDK both contains its own proxy relay functionality, and it initializes additional proxy SDKs from affiliates. Upon device registration to the C2, 

com.gaganode.sdk.node.endpoint.a
receives incoming packets from relay servers and places them in queue for the client to read and proxy through its exit node socket. The service manages multiple proxy sessions at once (referred to as clients), and each client has its own tcp/udp queue for messages.

We observe GaGaNode initializing PopaNet/NetNut and EarnFM Fleet residential proxy SDKs. GaGaNode/IPCola is thus likely able to further monetize its SDK and offer these affiliates access to the infected exit nodes.

NetNut / Popanet

Popanet is a residential proxy SDK developed by NetNut, a residential proxy operator. The GaGaNode module initiates the Popanet SDK (

io.popanet.Popa
). This malware is identical to the malware described in our previous disruption of NetNut. All C2 infrastructure used by Popanet samples connected to 
x.cpe
was taken down as part of the earlier Netnut disruption.

Traffmonetizer

The Traffmonetizer SDK is initialized inside the primary background service com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService. CoreService operation depends on the availability of policy JSON provided by the XCPE backdoor via IPC. Before calling Traffmonetizer SDK initialization methods, the application obtains a Traffmonetizer SDK API key from the native library 

libnative_keys.so
by calling its 
getTraffmonetizerKey()
function. 

Traffmonetizer functionality is split between two components where the Android SDK acts as a state machine which handles native library callbacks through asynchronous event dispatchers. 

ServiceBloc
monitors connection status updates from the native callbacks and 
ConnectivityBloc
monitors Wi-Fi and mobile data network changes. 

Traffmonetizer native library initialization and configuration is followed by a call to 

baseClientStart()
which establishes a WebSocket connection to a C2 server. Traffmonetizer uses a single WebSocket (TLS) connection to the command and control server to multiplex control messages and tunneled connections (supports both TCP and UDP). Traffmonetizer also supports “Content Delivery” tunneling which allows nodes to tunnel bandwidth-intensive traffic.

EarnFM

EarnFM is a residential proxy provider, and Fleet SDK is the provider’s SDK that enrolls devices as exit nodes into the proxy network. In 

com.abc.nexus
, FleetSDK is initialized by 
com.gaganode.sdk
as mentioned above. FleetSdk then loads native binary 
libfleetshare.so
. 

FleetSDK establishes a persistent WebSocket connection with its primary C2 server for routing arbitrary network traffic. Incoming tasking frames are received over the WebSocket channel and processed in a continuous loop. Messages contain structured JSON commands instructing the daemon to connect to specific remote hosts, with support for both TCP and UDP.

Backdoor Modules

Spirit

Spirit is a dynamic code loading backdoor. Spirit employs multiple stages. The first stage payload fetches device information (hardware, operating system, and manufacturer/brand information and geolocation), posting it over HTTP to a hardcoded C2 server, and fetches a list of additional modules to download from the server. The second stage communicates with a separate server, and is used for tasking, config sync, module retrieval, heartbeats, and reporting. We have observed Spirit loading a significant amount of additional malware monetization modules, including some of the families already directly loaded by 

com.abc.nexus
.

Moyu

Moyu is a 3-stage backdoor previously observed as part of the BadBox enterprise. On 

x.cpe
-backdoored devices, we observed it initialized by 
com.abc.nexus.service.DevourService.
The first stage is an offline dropper that reconstructs and loads an embedded second stage. Stage two polls an update C2 to download, decrypt, and load the third stage. Stage three implements a backdoor with hidden Double-WebView click/conversion fraud, persistent clipboard hijacking, and secondary dynamically loaded JAR execution and a separate residential proxy trojan.

Bird

Bird is a 2-stage backdoor previously tied to the BadBox enterprise. Stage 1 beacons a device and analysis-environment profile to its C2 server and, when the server approves, downloads, decrypts, and loads the Stage 2 JAR. Stage 2 implements a dynamic code loading backdoor (two plugin loaders plus a C2-driven reflective method invoker), a separate downloader (silent APK installation and Accessibility-driven Google Play installs), and ad abuse (lockscreen ads, overlays, browser launches).

Fission

Fission is a dynamic code loading (DCL) backdoor embedded within standard video applications (e.g., 

com.newtv.cboxtv
). Upon initialization, the first stage plugin contacts its C2 server to download additional modules. The decrypted second stage payload fetches execution targets and tracking URLs from the C2. The request sends an unencrypted POST request with tracking metrics from the internal 
DeviceManager.

The payload we observed was configured to commit ad fraud. Rather than rendering visible advertisements in a 

WebView
or UI component, the Stage 2 plugin executes headlessly in the background. The module queries ad server endpoints in the background to retrieve ad placement responses, parses out both primary impression beacons (
pvm
) and third-party tracking monitor URLs (
pvtpm
), and immediately fires HTTP GET requests to each tracking endpoint to register a fake ad view without displaying creative content. When executing inside specific smart-TV application stores (
com.changhong.appstore
or 
com.tcl.appmarket2
), the plugin initializes and triggers the ad SDK directly to report synthetic ad exposures.

Ad-Fraud

HiddenView

We observed HiddenView loaded remotely from the attacker’s Github channel as 

com.ota.service
. It is a standalone ad fraud application capable of running in the background using a transparent window overlay, using hidden WebViews to load targeted web pages and simulate user interaction (scrolling, clicking, typing, media playback), playing media unattended, and capturing the user’s screen.

How the pieces come together

Configuration messages pushed via MQTT (action 

ext/lib/config
) demonstrate how 
x.cpe
, 
com.abc.nexus
and various monetization modules function together. 

Upon registration, subscribed devices receive a

Infrastructure

As previously mentioned, devices first connect to various endpoints on 

*.anyevonline[.]com
for initial bootstrap, registration, and configuration. Earlier malware versions used various hostnames of 
{*tms | *ott | *ota}.szbboys[.]com
for the same purpose. 

While earlier versions of the malware used HTTP for C2, and then a blended C2 approach with both HTTP and MQTT, static analysis of current versions indicate they exclusively send/receive C2 communications via MQTT. A single MQTT broker orchestrates all MQTT C2 communications for samples we’ve identified. Hostname 

mqtt.szbboys[.]com
is resolved by hosts
 219.134.163[.]210
and 
219.134.163[.]211.
It listens on non-standard MQTT ports 3885-3887. 

The malware constructs OkHttp requests for file downloads after tasking via the MQTT broker. Files are hosted on several services:

  • Several Github release pages

  • The 

    filemail[.]com
    file sharing service

  • Two operator-controlled servers hosted on IPs

     38.145.197[.]135
    and 
    23.94.49[.]57

Netflow telemetry on the broker nodes (

219.134.163[.]210/.211
) indicates that while infected devices communicate over ports 3885–3887, operators likely manage the broker and dispatch tasking via interactive HTTP REST API (port 8082), WebSocket (port 8083), and EMQX web administration console (port 18083) sessions originating from non-bot IP space. 

Call to Action

While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry, and the broader technology ecosystem.

Accountability and Reform

A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust. By turning everyday hardware into persistent beachheads for criminal affiliates, Videostrong prioritized illicit post-sale recurring revenue over the safety and privacy of its users. Downstream hardware brands, white-label resellers, telecommunications providers, and online e-commerce marketplaces also share responsibility for closing this vector. Retailers and distributors should require independent security audits from Original Design Manufacturers (ODMs) and swiftly delist manufacturers implicated in supply-chain abuse.

Residential proxy providers have been able to flourish under the guise of legitimate businesses. While some providers may claim to behave ethically and only enroll devices with the clear consent of consumers, any claims of "ethical sourcing" must be backed by transparent, auditable proof of user consent. In our analysis, these proxy operators only seek consent when they are forced due to platform policy and enforcement. Silent opt-in without user consent remains the most prevalent means by which devices are turned into exit nodes.

Empowering and Protecting the Consumer

Residential proxies are an understudied area of risk for consumers, and more can be done to raise awareness. Consumers should be extremely wary of applications that offer payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your internet." These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device’s home network. We urge users to stick to app stores you trust, review permissions for third-party VPNs and proxies, and ensure built-in security protections like Google Play Protect are active.

Consumers should only purchase connected devices, such as set-top boxes, from reputable manufacturers. Our Android TV website provides the most up-to-date list of partners.

Industry Collaboration

We encourage mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces and other tech platforms to continue sharing intelligence and implementing best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software and limit their harms.

Oct 26 - Oct 30

  • Simplify PostgreSQL Monitoring with the New AlloyDB Omni Web UI

    Semantic model routing replaces rigid static paths with a lightweight helper model to dynamically classify and dispatch intent-driven LLM traffic. Join Saravanakumar Rajagopal on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 5:00 PM CET for a Community TechTalk exploring how to leverage Antigravity and skills to architect these intelligent multi-provider routing patterns natively inside Apigee. Discover how to optimize your AI infrastructure and enhance flexibility at scale.

    Register for the November 12 Community TechTalk

Oct 19 - Oct 23

Using declarative workflows in Apigee, teams can spin up a fully governed LLM gateway in minutes using a few environment variables. Join Luis Cuellar on Thursday, October 29, 2026 for a Community TechTalk exploring end-to-end AI workflows. Discover how to layer essential defenses—including Model Armor for prompt protection, Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) for sensitive data redaction, rate limiting, and response caching—before routing autonomous agent interactions through your gateway filters.

    Register for the October 29 Community TechTalk

Because agents plan their actions on the fly, permanent admin access means one hallucination can cascade into production. Join us on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 8:30 AM PST to see how Google CloudPrivileged Access Manager (PAM) brings Zero Standing Privileges to AI delegation, putting humans in command with cloud-native control that doesn't slow developers down.

    Register for the November 18 webinar

You can now route Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding without modifying your API spec or managing a split estate. This update also strengthens integration with the Gemini platform, allowing you to stream responses from Gemini, Claude, and OpenAI gpt-oss models seamlessly while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability.

    Read the blog to get started

Oct 12 - Oct 16

Join Tarun Abraham on Thursday, November 5, 2026 for a Community TechTalk on AI tokenomics. Discover how to use Apigee to enforce isolated, tiered token budgets and model access for each team—such as assigning Engineering a dedicated budget for Gemini Pro while covering mixed usage for Marketing—without changing application code. Discover how to build an Intelligent AI Gateway using Apigee X to dynamically evaluate prompt complexity in real-time. This new blueprint automatically routes simple queries to lightweight models (like Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite) and complex reasoning tasks to advanced models (like Gemini 3.7 Flash), achieving over 70% cost savings without sacrificing output quality.

entries.title: When the Kubernetes API went silent: A three-layer networking mystery
entries.summary: Every support engineer has a case that stays with them. The one that comes up at team lunches. The one where, even after it's resolved, you find yourself staring at a packet capture at midnight just to make sure you really understand what happened. This is that case. It started in January 2026 with a support ticket that read deceptively simply: pods are intermittently failing to reach the Kubernet
entries.content:
Akash Thakur

Sr. Technical Solutions Engineer

Every support engineer has a case that stays with them. The one that comes up at team lunches. The one where, even after it's resolved, you find yourself staring at a packet capture at midnight just to make sure you really understand what happened. This is that case.

It started in January 2026 with a support ticket that read deceptively simply: pods are intermittently failing to reach the Kubernetes API server. The error was a familiar-looking timeout. The customer had already ruled out their own operators. What none of us knew yet was that we were looking at three separate bugs — in three different layers of the stack — all conspiring to produce the same symptom at the same time.

By the time it was over, around 800 developers had been blocked from deploying to production for weeks on end, and GKE clusters across europe-west had ground to a halt. In a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself.

This is the story of how we got there.

Part one: The alarm bell that wouldn't stop

The customer ran a large multi-cluster GKE environment in Google Cloud's europe-west region. Their clusters used Private Service Connect — Google Cloud's mechanism for exposing the GKE control plane privately — and had a rich ecosystem of system-level workloads: Twistlock security scanners, External Secrets Operator for secrets management, Cilium for network policy, as well as several internal Kubernetes operators.

The first errors appeared in one of its user acceptance testing (UAT) clusters in europe-west, and a few days later in a second cluster in the same region. They looked like this:

Application logs — pods across multiple namespaces

Initially the errors were intermittent — spikes in the logs, not a hard outage. The customer suspected their own code. Their team had recently deployed a custom operator built with the kopf framework, and it was the first thing they looked at. But the logs showed the errors had started eight days before the operator was ever deployed. When they shut it down completely, the timeouts kept coming.

The issue persists even after completely scaling down the External Secrets Operator. The errors are appearing from customer workloads, and system-level pods we haven't touched.

The growing list of suspects

When a case like this arrives, the first instinct is to ask: what changed? The customer's timeline gave us several candidates, and we worked through them methodically.

  • The custom operator (kopf): Ruled out immediately — errors predated deployment by a week and continued after shutdown.

  • External Secrets Operator: Removed entirely on customer request. Timeouts continued in customer workloads that relied on Kubernetes control plane (KCP) connectivity, and cluster-internal system pods.

  • Security agents: Uninstalled. Same result. We were now watching system-level Kubernetes components fail to reach their own control plane.

  • conntrack table exhaustion: One theory was that too many half-open connections were filling the OS connection tracking table on the control plane nodes. We checked. The conntrack table was at roughly 50% capacity — of a default maximum of 1.3M entries. Not even close to exhaustion.

  • Control plane overload: We scaled up the KCP VM size. kube-apiserver latencies looked healthy. No improvement on the timeout side.

What made this case genuinely strange was the scope. We confirmed the timeouts were happening across five different clusters, affecting DaemonSets, Deployments, and system pods alike. External clients — developer laptops, GitHub Actions runners — were also hitting the same wall. This was not a broken workload. This was something wrong with the path between everything and the API server.

The timeline so far

  • Day 1: First I/O timeout errors appear (One of the UAT clusters in europe-west3. Intermittent, easy to dismiss.)

  • Day 10: Errors become persistent (Frequency increases significantly. The issue is no longer dismissible.)

  • Day 15: Case escalated — P0 bug filed (Multiple clusters confirmed affected. ~800 developers blocked. Production releases are frozen. Formal escalation begins.)

  • Day 20: All obvious suspects ruled out (Custom operator, security agents, conntrack exhaustion, control plane resizing — all cleared.)

  • Day 22: Packet captures collected (Captures taken simultaneously at the control-plane node NIC and from inside the kube-api container. The investigation enters its most critical phase.)

With the obvious suspects cleared, and the scope undeniably wide, we did what you do when the application layer has nothing left to say: We went to the packets.

Part two: Tracing the ghost in the wire

To understand what the packet captures revealed, you first need to understand the architecture that a GKE pod traverses when it makes an API call. In a Private Service Connect-based GKE cluster, the path is deceptively long for something that looks like a local connection.

(Note for formatting: Consider including the Pod → kube-apiserver flow diagram here: Pod -> Worker Node -> PSC NAT+Proxy -> ILB -> KCP VM NIC -> kube-apiserver)

The key component here is Private Service Connect. When a pod dials 1.2.3.4:443, it is not actually going directly to the control plane; that IP is a virtual endpoint. The connection is intercepted by Google's networking fabric, NAT'd through a Private Service Connect endpoint, passed through an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer, and ultimately delivered to the KCP VM, where Envoy acts as a local proxy in front of the actual kube-apiserver process.

Private Service Connect adds a proxy protocol header to each new connection, so the kube-apiserver can see the real client IP. This will turn out to be important later.

What the packets revealed

When we captured simultaneously at the KCP VM's NIC (the PIGv interface, Google's programmable virtual NIC) and from inside the kube-apiserver container, we saw something striking.

SYN packets from the pods were arriving at the KCP VM's NIC. They were getting that far. But instead of receiving a SYN-ACK in response — the expected second step of a TCP handshake — the client was getting back an out-of-place ACK. Not an RST. Not silence. An ACK that logically belonged to a different, earlier connection.

Wireshark, the network protocol analyzer, was flagging these streams with a label that initially seemed innocuous: "TCP Port numbers reused."

Wireshark — packet stream showing the failed handshake

The pattern was clear. Something was causing the KCP VM to respond to a fresh SYN with an ACK that belonged to a different connection that had ended minutes ago. The old connection had used the same source port (53426 in the example above), and the KCP VM had never fully let go of it.

"The KCP server sends FIN,ACK; client responds with FIN,ACK and then ACK. But KCP receives ACK before FIN,ACK. KCP server never ACKs the FIN,ACK — continuous retransmission of ACK. RST does not clear state."

The "Invalid ACK" spike

While one thread of the investigation was analyzing packet captures, a.k.a., pcaps, another team was digging into internal metrics for the Private Service Connect infrastructure — specifically the user space packet switch (USPS), Google's software switching layer that handles NAT and proxy protocol header injection for Private Service Connect connections.

They found something alarming in the metrics for Andromeda, Google's networking fabric. A counter called "Proxy protocol drop: invalid ACK packet" had been flat for months — and then, in February 2026, it spiked sharply upward to several drops per second across the affected europe-west regions.

That date matched a USPS version rollout. This version included a change which was a fix for a different bug but something about it had changed the behavior of how Private Service Connect handled a specific class of packet.

Challenge ACKs: The RFC 5961 mechanism

To understand the next piece of the puzzle, we need to talk about a TCP security mechanism called the challenge ACK, defined in RFC 5961.

Imagine a TCP connection has closed — gone through the FIN/ACK dance and terminated. The server-side (here, the KCP VM) may still briefly remember the connection's sequence numbers in its TCP state machine. Now imagine that shortly afterward, a new client connection arrives on the same source port and destination port (the same 5-tuple). From the kernel's perspective, this could be a stale packet from the old connection, or it could be an attacker trying to inject data into what the kernel thinks is still an open session.

RFC 5961 says: when you receive a SYN that matches an existing or recently-closed connection's remembered state, don't accept it blindly. Send a challenge ACK — an acknowledgment that carries the last known sequence number of the old connection. If the new client is legitimate, it will see this unexpected ACK, recognize the connection is stale, and send a RST to clear the state. The server then accepts the next SYN normally.

The challenge ACK flow — how it's supposed to work

This mechanism works perfectly — when the challenge ACK is allowed through. But that was exactly what the new USPS change was blocking.

The culprit: A well-intentioned fix

The change in USPS had been designed to fix a legitimate security issue in Private Service Connect's proxy protocol handling. Part of its effect was to drop packets it classified as "invalid ACKs" during the connection handshake phase — specifically, ACKs that arrived before the initial SYN-ACK had been sent, which in normal circumstances would be anomalous.

Unfortunately, challenge ACKs look exactly like this: They arrive from the server before the new handshake has completed, in response to a SYN. From the USPS's new perspective, they looked like invalid packets. They were dropped silently.

Why this broke GKE specifically: Private Service Connect uses NAT to share a single public endpoint across many client pods. This means many different pods — running on different nodes, from different namespaces — can all end up using the same source port after NAT, creating a high rate of 5-tuple collisions. The challenge ACK mechanism was being triggered far more often than it would be in a normal direct-connection scenario. The USPS fix hadn't introduced challenge ACKs — they had always been there. It had introduced the dropping of them, which broke a flow that GKE's TCP stack had silently depended on to clear stale state.

Mitigation: Rolling back the change

In February, we rolled back the USPS change, restoring the old behavior where challenge ACKs were passed through instead of dropped. The rate of "Proxy protocol drop: invalid ACK packet" dropped back toward baseline almost immediately.

By early March , 2026, the customer confirmed that all affected clusters had recovered. No more timeout errors.

But the rollback wasn't a fix. It was a band-aid. It restored the behavior the system had accidentally depended on. The deeper question — why was the KCP VM in FIN_WAIT_2 for over two minutes in the first place? — was still completely unanswered.

That question led to Part 3. And it's where things got genuinely strange.

Part three: Three bugs, one crime scene

The mitigation bought us time, but it left a question hanging in the air: Why did the KCP VM keep connections in FIN_WAIT_2 for so long? A well-behaved TCP stack processes a FIN, acknowledges it, and closes the connection. The KCP VM was failing to do this, leaving half-open connections that persisted for more than two minutes — long enough for the port to be reused by Private Service Connect's NAT layer, long enough to cause the challenge ACK scenario we'd uncovered.

To answer this, we needed to understand not just one bug, but three distinct failure modes that had intersected at the worst possible moment.

Bug #1: Packet reordering at the PIGv

The first piece was discovered through careful analysis of simultaneous captures at two points: the KCP VM's host NIC (inside the physical host running the VM) versus the PIGv — the virtual NIC as seen by the VM.

At the host NIC level, packets arrived in perfect order. But by the time they crossed through USPS and appeared at the PIGv, they had been subtly reordered.

This happens because of how Private Service Connect's miss-thread processing works. When Private Service Connect intercepts a new flow it hasn't seen before (a "miss"), it processes that packet through a slower path that adds the proxy protocol header and sets up NAT state. Subsequent packets in the same flow take a fast path. The consequence: a FIN or RST packet belonging to a flow in mid-close might arrive slightly out of order relative to the ACKs that followed it.

What the KCP VM actually received (reordered sequence)

The reordering put the client's FIN after the server had already sent its own FIN. The server entered FIN_WAIT_1, then FIN_WAIT_2 after seeing the client's ACK of the server's FIN. But then the client's own FIN arrived — and the server's kernel ignored it.

Bug #2: Envoy's half-close and the frozen timer

Why couldn't the operating system clean up on its own? There is a Linux kernel parameter called tcp_fin_timeout that governs exactly this: how long a socket in FIN_WAIT_2 waits before being forcibly closed. On the KCP VM, this was set to 60 seconds.

But tcp_fin_timeout only applies to orphaned sockets — sockets that no process is currently holding open. Envoy, the proxy that sits in front of kube-apiserver on the KCP VM, was performing a half-close: it called shutdown(SHUT_WR), which closes the write side of the connection but keeps the socket open so it can still receive data. This is perfectly valid TCP behavior and is how graceful half-duplex termination is supposed to work.

The side effect: As long as Envoy held the socket with SHUT_WR, the kernel did not consider it orphaned. tcp_fin_timeout never started. The socket sat in FIN_WAIT_2 indefinitely, waiting for a client FIN it would never be able to process correctly.

Kernel socket state — captured via netstat just before a new connection

Bug #3: The Linux kernel's silent failure

But there was still a missing piece. Even with the reordered FIN, a healthy kernel should still process a received FIN in FIN_WAIT_2 and move to TIME_WAIT. The socket should eventually close. Why wasn't it?

This led us deep into the Linux TCP state-machine implementation. When the reordered client FIN arrived at the KCP VM, the kernel's tcp_ack() function was called to process it. And here, in kernel version 6.1 (which underpinned the Container-Optimized OS (COS) running on the KCP VMs), there was a bug.

RFC 5961 added stricter validation for acceptable ACK numbers — specifically, an ACK could be considered valid even if it was slightly "old" (within a sequence number window), to handle network reordering. But in kernel 6.1, there was a code path where tcp_ack() returned zero — indicating "this packet was not fully processed" — when it encountered an ACK that was old but within the RFC 5961 acceptable window. The caller of tcp_ack() in the FIN processing path checked this return value, saw zero, and did… nothing. The FIN was received and silently discarded.

The Linux kernel commit that fixed it (upstream)

The bug had existed since kernel 6.1 and was already fixed in kernel 6.9.7 — but GKE's KCP VMs were running COS builds based on 6.1 and 6.6. The fix needed to be backported and shipped as a COS image update.

How the three bugs combined

Individually, none of these three issues would have caused an outage of this magnitude. It took all three acting together to create the failure:

  • Bug #1 alone: Packet reordering is mildly disruptive, but the kernel would normally still eventually process the FIN and clean up, just slower than ideal.

  • Bug #2 alone: Envoy's half-close is perfectly correct behavior. It only becomes a problem if the FIN is never properly processed.

  • Bug #3 alone: The kernel's failure to process old-but-acceptable ACKs would cause some connections to linger, but the impact would be limited without the port-reuse pressure from Private Service Connect NAT.

  • All three together: Reordering causes the FIN to arrive out of sequence; the kernel bug prevents it from being processed; Envoy's SHUT_WR prevents the timeout from firing; the socket stays in FIN_WAIT_2 indefinitely. Private Service Connect NAT reuses the port. challenge ACK is sent. The USPS fix drops it. Connection fails.

The resolution: A three-pronged fix

Resolving this required action at three different levels, coordinated across multiple teams over several weeks:

  • Immediate mitigation (Feb, 2026): Rollback of change in USPS. Restored the previous behavior where challenge ACKs were forwarded rather than dropped. Customer clusters recovered by early March.

  • Correctness fix: A replacement change to handle the challenge ACK scenario properly in the Private Service Connect proxy protocol layer, rather than simply restoring the old drop behavior. A PacketDrill test was added to the test suite to prevent regression.

  • Root cause fix — Linux kernel patch: Upstream patch ("net: tcp: accept old ack during closing"), authored by Eric Dumazet. Merged into Linux 6.9.7. Backported to 6.6.y and 6.1.y LTS branches. — shipping in GKE 1.33.5 and later. The bug is fully resolved at the OS level for all GKE versions running these COS images.

What made this case different

Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete.

What finally cracked it was the discipline of simultaneous packet capture at multiple points in the path. Without captures at the host NIC, the PIGv, and inside the container at the same time, we would never have seen the reordering. Without correlating those pcaps to the USPS metric spike on February 18, we would never have found the dropped challenge ACKs. And without reproducing the issue in a lab environment, we would never have found the kernel bug that made the FIN_WAIT_2 state permanent.

The other thing that made this work was the team. Over the course of two weeks, engineers from seven or eight different specialties contributed: GKE networking, Private Service Connect infrastructure, Hostnet, Andromeda, KCP, and ultimately the kernel community. No single person could have held all of this in their head. The case notes, the shared bug tracker, the meticulously collected pcaps — they were the connective tissue that let a distributed team work as one.

In the end, the customer got back to production. The kernel got a better bug fix. And the rest of us got a very good story about why packet reordering, half-closed sockets, and a well-intentioned security patch should never be allowed in the same room at the same time.

This blog is based on real case data from an anonymized customer support engagement and internal bugs. The Linux kernel fix referenced is commit 795a7dfbc3d9, authored by Eric Dumazet. Special thanks to the engineers across GKE, Private Service Connect, Hostnet, Andromeda, COS, and the Linux networking community whose work made this resolution possible.

entries.content:
Shruthi Nambi

Senior Product Manager

Today, we’re announcing that spend caps on Google Cloud Budgets are generally available.

With this release, we’re delivering ways to protect your workloads from runaway costs without risking resource deletion. More importantly, we’re introducing three major updates, directly inspired by your feedback since the initial preview, to bring programmability, real-time visibility, and automated guardrails to your cost-control playbook.

How the new spend caps can help your business

We have significantly enhanced the usability and power of spend caps in three ways:

1. Automation through spend caps API: Managing guardrails manually across hundreds of projects is a major operational challenge. To address this, we have launched the spend caps API, which can be accessed from the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API. You can now programmatically enforce your financial boundaries for eligible services within each project, without additional overhead. You can automatically lift, update, or delete caps on the fly and instantly apply a spend cap whenever a developer spins up a new sandbox project.

2. Real-time visibility with live cost reports: Spend caps for AI services trigger within minutes of usage using estimated, live costs. When a cap triggers, you need to know exactly why and when the limit was breached. You can now view these faster, estimated costs directly inside your Cost Reports. Instead of waiting hours for standard billing pipelines to settle net costs, you get the exact financial snapshots that triggered the enforcement, giving you the immediate context needed to run a precise root-cause analysis.

3. Automated guardrails for your monthly resets: Before, once a spend cap was triggered, the usage block remained locked until you manually lifted it in the UI. Today, we are introducing automated monthly resets. You no longer need to worry about manually lifting caps every month. Enforced spend caps will automatically reset, and blocked services will seamlessly resume at the beginning of the next month. However, if your governance policies require a strict manual audit before resuming operations, the manual override option continues to exist exactly as before.

Best practices for deploying spend caps

As you roll out spend caps across your organization, keep these operational tips in mind:

  • Target non-production environments first: Start by applying strict, low-dollar spend caps to your developer sandboxes, testing clusters, and experimental AI agent playgrounds.
  • Configure alerts wisely: Default alerts are automatically sent to billing administrators and project owners at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the cap. Make sure the right folks are set up in these roles. This ensures your team is never caught off guard when a budget is nearing depletion. Spend caps permissions can also be added to custom roles, if needed.
  • Understand fixed vs on-demand costs: Spend caps halt pay-as-you-go and CUD-covered requests once the budget threshold is hit. However, Provisioned Throughput is never halted; requests using reserved capacity will continue to run, and serve traffic normally.

Refresher on GCP’s dual-pronged defense playbook

Spend Caps work seamlessly alongside our native Early Anomalies Detection to provide a closed-loop defense for your cloud spend. Read our previous blog for a detailed explanation on how to use these tools to effortlessly set up a GCP defense playbook. 

Get started today

Spend caps are now ready to support your workloads at scale. Read our documentation for more details and navigate to the Budgets and Alerts page in your Google Cloud Billing Console, to set your first spend cap. 

To integrate programmatic guardrails into your deployment workflows, check out our newly published spend caps API documentation.

entries.content:
Alex Barrett

Editor, Google Cloud blog

Dave Bartoletti

Product Manager, AI & Computing Infrastructure

The Google Cloud AI Infrastructure team had another busy month in October, filled with new product launches and updates to power today’s AI and agentic workloads scalably and efficiently. We were also honored to share our progress with customers, partners, and the broader community at leading industry events, including NVIDIA GTC, PyTorch Conference, and AGNTCon + MCPCon. Let’s dive in!

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • New compute service: Agent Compute Engine is a purpose-built compute service providing high-performance, hardware-isolated microVM sandboxes alongside expanded agent governance capabilities like Agent Gateway and Agent Registry, all in the service of securing and scaling autonomous AI agents. Its primary benefits include rapid sub-second activation, extreme workload density through copy-on-write memory sharing, enterprise-grade security and identity management, and cross-cloud observability.

  • AI Hypercomputer updates: At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 we announced updates to our agentic infrastructure, including to A5X instances powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, Virgo Network scale-out fabric, and Managed Lustre storage. These co-engineered advancements provide enterprises with accelerated performance, enhanced sovereign AI controls, while advanced Confidential Computing capabilities help you train and deploy complex multi-step models securely and efficiently.

  • GKE product update: CPU startup boost for GKE, in preview, uses Kubernetes In-place Pod Resize to dynamically elevate container CPU resources during initialization and scale them back down to steady-state levels without having to restart the containers. This feature removes startup throttling and accelerates cold starts by up to 2x for demanding workloads, helping to lower cloud infrastructure costs.

  • GKE product update: The preview of the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters.

  • Modernization tools: Together at last. Google Cloud Modernize brings Google Cloud’s migration and modernization tools, including Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine, Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization and our new EKS-to-GKE Migration Agent, into a single portfolio. Enterprise teams now have purpose-built agentic capabilities across infrastructure assessment, platform modernization, and application modernization.

  • Cloud Run product update: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run automatically scale worker pools based on Temporal task queue demands and scale down to zero when idle. This integration eliminates cluster management, lowers costs, using Temporal Worker Versioning to safely handle stateful, long-running workflows and AI agent workloads.

  • New open-source product: llm-d 1.0 is an open-source, Kubernetes-native serving stack that turns a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool, unifying distributed LLM inference across mixed Google Cloud TPU and GPU fleets. Co-founded by Google and partners, it provides production-ready benefits such as cache-aware routing, tiered KV cache offloading, and priority-based flow control to dramatically improve context reuse, reduce time-to-first-token latency, and efficiently scale multi-tenant agent workloads.

  • New open-source product: Working with Meta, we open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack that integrates Google TPUs directly into the PyTorch ecosystem alongside GPUs and CPUs. Now developers can train, serve, and deploy models natively on TPUs using familiar frameworks like Hugging Face, vLLM, and TorchTitan.

  • Google Distributed Cloud updates: Organizations that operate under strict sovereignty mandates would love to use AI to help them process data, but can’t send it to the cloud. The latest version of Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped brings frontier AI models and multimodal enterprise search with Gemini into these isolated environments. In addition, GDC air-gapped supports NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture, and features enhanced networking and security capabilities. 

  • Edge inference product: Google open-sourced ML Drift, a cross-platform on-device GPU compute engine built for LiteRT that abstracts hardware complexities across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU. The framework delivers peak performance, enhanced 5D tensor support, and memory efficiency for both classical machine learning workloads and advanced generative AI models at the edge.

  • Open-weight model support: Reflection's Beam is an open-weight, 501-parameter model released under an Apache 2.0 license designed specifically for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. We announced day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for service Beam on AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure.

Practitioner guides and how-tos

  • AI network reference architectures: In Networking for AI inference model serving - GKE only and for all other backends, learn about reference architectures for AI inference model serving that provide centralized governance and private IP routing using Private Service Connect, Apigee API Management, and Model Armor. These architectures simplify multi-model scaling and prompt security across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid clouds. 

  • How-to guide: A Tale of TPU Observability on GKE: Part 2 - Dynamic Slicing Enhancements breaks down GKE's new Dynamic Slicing observability tools and metrics for next-generation v7 TPUs through an engaging, story-driven observability guide featuring Alex, a lead AI platform engineer. Explore the step-by-step diagnostic workflows with real-world examples and handy command-line snippets. Check out Part 1 here.

Customer and partner updates

  • AI21 achieves an 83% reduction in time-to-start for AI workloads with AI Hypercomputer: Frontier lab AI21 needed a new stack on which to train its Jamba family, and chose AI Hypercomputer configured with GKE on A3 and A3 Ultra instances. By doing so, AI21 says it cut high-priority job wait times from 72 hours to 12, and manual scheduling interventions from 20 per week to zero.

  • Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs: Visko, an AI startup developing interactive world models, deployed an end-to-end live inference pipeline that combines video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio onto a single Cloud TPU slice. In this blog, the team discusses how it engineered the pipeline, the architectural optimizations it made, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI.

  • ZenteiQ scales physical AI inference 4x with GKE and llm-d: In order to pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, Indian AI startup ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs. GKE and GKE Inference Gateway gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators.

  • Palo Alto Networks modernizes cloud-delivered security service: Palo Alto has worked with Google Cloud since 2018 to deliver its Prisma Access security service, and it was time to update it. In order not to compromise its security guarantees, Palo Alto separated the platform into two independently scalable layers: an ingress layer that handles traffic routing and forwarding running on GKE, with Axion C4A instances; and a security layer that handles threat inspection, running on dedicated single-tenant VMs fronted by an Internal Load Balancer. Each layer can now scale, update, and operate independently. 

  • Oracle is the first hyperscaler to provide TPUs outside Google Cloud: By deploying Google TPUs, Oracle is broadening the range of AI chips available through its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), and giving customers more options for running AI workloads. Google TPUs on OCI will be available in 2027.

Research, reports and deep-dives

  • New resource: As enterprise organizations shift from isolated AI experiments to production-scale systems, different departments — from engineering and finance to executive leadership — often speak different technical dialects; The Encyclopedia of AI Infrastructure bridges that communication gap by demystifying complex infrastructure jargon.

  • Analyst report: We are thrilled to announce that Google was named a Leader in the inaugural 2026 IDC MarketScape for Agentic AI Platforms. 

  • Deep dive: A companion technical guide describing the architecture of Agent Compute Engine and how Google’s Gemini team needed both the isolation of a VM and the speed and density of a container to deliver personal agents for every Gemini user.

September 2026

Product, technology, and tools updates

Google Kubernetes Engine updates: The GKE team is all about improving the scalability of the platform, and in September, those improvements came in many shapes and sizes:

  • New feature: Need an execution runtime with higher density for your agentic workloads? We engineered the new open-source GKE Agent Substrate to run millions of sandboxes with 10x higher density than standard container runtimes. Agent Substrate also delivers sub-500ms resume operations at over 500 suspend/resume activations per second with a native zero-trust kernel and network isolation. 

  • Product update: GKE now has scale-to-zero capabilities built-in. No need to configure complex components to scale your workloads down, thanks to the HPA with the Autoscaling Metric and support for KEP-2021, which do the job for you, out of the box. Read the blog to learn more. 

  • Product update: Further, the GKE HPA (with the above-mentioned Autoscaling Metric) now lets you scale up and down based on custom PromQL metrics, in addition to standard metrics, allowing you to trigger workloads according to conditions that are meaningful and unique to your business. Read more here. 

  • New feature: Yet another scalability feature is GKE Pod snapshots, which lets you save the running state of your workload, including CPU and GPU memory, and restore it on demand. According to internal tests, GKE Pod snapshots can reduce AI inference start-up by as much as 89%. Learn more here.

  • New migration tool: Finally, if you’ve always wanted to migrate your container workloads from AWS EKS to GKE but feared a daunting, high-friction engineering endeavor, we’ve just launched GKE agentic migration, a purpose-built agent plugin that replaces brittle, ad-hoc prompting with an AI-assisted migration pipeline protected by deterministic guardrails. Designed as a compilation of agent skills and a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, it uses AI to translate complex AWS EKS IaC and Kubernetes manifests directly into GKE landing zones. Get started with the onboarding guide.

  • Feature updates: Reinforcement learning (RL) and evaluation workloads are a beast: In a standard agentic RL loop, an LLM policy generates actions like code snippets on GPUs and executes them inside isolated CPU sandboxes to observe a reward signal. To help, we developed GKE Agent Sandbox optimized for RL, plus an Agent Sandbox RL orchestration SDK and native integrations for popular RL gyms and harnesses. All are now generally available, and you can learn more here.

Request access to the preview here. 

  • New product: If you run generative AI and RAG data layers  — think Milvus, Pinecone, Qdrant, Vespa, Redis, and in-memory context caching — you may want to take a look at the M4N family of VMs, now GA, which offers the highest per-core IOPS and throughput of leading hyperscalers. Paired with Google Cloud's custom Titanium offload architecture and paired with Hyperdisk Extreme, M4N instances deliver up to 25,000 MiB/s (25 GiB/s) of aggregate host storage performance and up to 1 million IOPS. 

  • New product: Another new Compute Engine product, Z4D, is GA, and a strong storage solution for AI/ML training and inference workloads. When configured as a bare metal instance, Z4D provides both the high local SSD (LSSD) capacity and low latency required by agentic microVMs, so you can run thousands of isolated sandboxes per host with native performance and efficiency. Learn about Z4D machines here.

  • Product update: Today’s AI training and inference pipelines create data faster than most storage management systems can keep up, creating challenges for teams trying to understand their storage estates. A new version of Storage Intelligence advisor makes it easier to answer the question: "What’s in my buckets?" and quickly identify unexpected changes. Then, enhanced batch operations let you automate bulk changes across your buckets — say, move storage classes, mass-delete stale or temporary data, or apply metadata, tagging, retention, or encryption changes. Learn about the latest in Storage Intelligence advisor here.

  • New product: Last but not least, a new version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL brings together pioneering Google infrastructure — Colossus distributed file system, and Jupiter network — to power a new, no-compromises database architecture for the agentic era.

At the edge, the multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway focuses on global, multi-region traffic distribution and high availability. Beneath that, the LLM-d router handles complex, memory-aware scheduling algorithms to keep utilization high. This architecture is deliberately runtime-, model-, and accelerator-agnostic, and in tests, routing traffic through the multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway added less than 1% overhead.

To get the most out of every dollar spent, you need to understand workload lifecycle metrics in GKE. This detailed guide explains how to turn opaque cluster behaviors into actionable telemetry.
